title: Towards best-case response times of real-time tasks under fixed-priority scheduling with preemption thresholds

extraction.paper_name: Towards best-case response times of real-time tasks under fixed-priority scheduling with preemption thresholds
extraction.paper_description: The paper investigates best-case response time (BRT) analysis for Fixed-Priority Scheduling with Preemption Thresholds (FPTS). It proves that for non-preemptive tasks, the BRT is simply the best-case computation time, and demonstrates that FPTS BRT analysis is more complex than Fixed-Priority Preemptive Scheduling (FPPS) due to interference from non-preempting higher-priority tasks.

formal_description.statement: A task set T consists of n independent periodic tasks tau_1, tau_2, ..., tau_n, where each task tau_i is characterized by (T_i, phi_i, WD_i, BD_i, WC_i, BC_i, pi_i, theta_i).

variables.WC_i: Worst-case computation time of task i
variables.BC_i: Best-case computation time of task i
variables.theta_i: Preemption threshold of task i, where pi_1 >= theta_i >= pi_i

assumptions: Higher pi_i value indicates higher priority
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fundamental task model for FPTS.

informal_sketch.intuition: Each task has a fixed priority and a threshold. A task can only be interrupted by tasks with a priority strictly higher than its threshold.
steps: Assign priority pi_i to each task
Assign threshold theta_i such that it is at least the task's own priority
If theta_i == pi_i, the system is fully preemptive (FPPS)
If theta_i == pi_max, the system is non-preemptive (FPNS)
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
class Task:
    def __init__(self, T, phi, WD, BD, WC, BC, pi, theta):
        self.T = T
        self.phi = phi
        self.WD = WD
        self.BD = BD
        self.WC = WC
        self.BC = BC
        self.pi = pi
        self.theta = theta

def can_preempt(task_h, task_i):
    return task_h.pi > task_i.theta
key_insights: FPTS generalizes both preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling.

formal_description.statement: For a job k of task tau_i, R_i_k = f_i_k - a_i_k, where R_i_k = S_i_k + H_i_k.

variables.R_i_k: Response time of job k of task i
variables.f_i_k: Finalization time of job k of task i
variables.a_i_k: Activation time of job k of task i

assumptions: Jobs do not start before previous jobs of the same task complete
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the components of a task's response time.

informal_sketch.intuition: The total time a task takes to finish is the time it waits to start plus the time it takes to execute (including preemptions).
steps: Calculate start delay S_i_k as the difference between start and activation
Calculate hold time H_i_k as the difference between finish and start
Sum them to get total response time
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_response_time(job):
    S_i_k = job.start_time - job.activation_time
    H_i_k = job.finish_time - job.start_time
    return S_i_k + H_i_k
key_insights: In non-preemptive scheduling, the hold time H_i_k is exactly the computation time.

variables.BR_i: Best-case response time of task i
variables.R_i_k_phi: Response time of job k under phasing phi

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the best-case response time as the minimum possible response time across all jobs and phasings.

informal_sketch.intuition: The best-case response time is the absolute minimum time any instance of a task takes to complete.
steps: Simulate or analyze all possible task phasings
Find the minimum response time across all jobs in the hyperperiod
key_insights: BR_i is the lower bound of task latency.

formal_description.statement: A task set T is schedulable iff for all i: BD_i <= BR_i AND WR_i <= WD_i.
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the condition for a real-time system to be considered correct.

informal_sketch.intuition: A system is only correct if tasks finish neither too early nor too late.
steps: Check if the shortest response time is at least the best-case deadline
Check if the longest response time is at most the worst-case deadline
key_insights: Schedulability in this context involves both upper and lower timing bounds.

variables.BU_T: Best-case utilization of task set T
variables.BC_i: Best-case computation time of task i

informal_sketch.intuition: The best-case utilization represents the minimum fraction of time the processor is busy.
steps: For each task, divide its minimum execution time by its period
Sum these values for the entire set
key_insights: If BU_T < 1, there must be idle time in the schedule.

formal_description.statement: If theta_i = pi_1 AND (BU_T < 1 OR (BU_T = 1 AND lcm_T exists)), then BR_i = BC_i.

variables.lcm_T: Least common multiple of all task periods

formal_description.conclusion: The best-case response time of a non-preemptive task is its best-case execution time.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a task cannot be preempted, its response time is just its execution time plus any delay before it starts. If there is idle time (BU_T < 1), we can always find a phasing where the task starts immediately upon activation.
steps: Identify that for non-preemptive tasks, hold time H_i_k = BC_i
Show that an idle interval exists if BU_T < 1
Shift task activations so that task i activates during an idle interval
Relative start time S_i_k becomes 0, so R_i_k = 0 + BC_i
key_insights: Non-preemptive tasks are independent of higher-priority interference in the best case.

formal_description.statement: Under FPPS and arbitrary deadlines, an optimal instant for task tau_i occurs when the completion of a job of tau_i coincides with the simultaneous activation of all its higher priority tasks.
formal_description.conclusion: Identifies the phasing that produces the best-case response time for FPPS.

informal_sketch.intuition: To get the shortest response time in preemptive scheduling, you want the task to finish just before a burst of high-priority tasks arrives, effectively 'escaping' their interference.
steps: Align the end of task i's execution with the start of all tasks in {tau_1...tau_i-1}
This specific job in the level-i active period will have the minimum R_i_k
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def find_fpps_optimal_instant(task_i, hp_tasks):
    # Hypothetical alignment
    job_finish_time = simultaneous_activation_time(hp_tasks)
    return job_finish_time
key_insights: The best-case job is the last job in the level-i active period for FPPS.

formal_description.statement: In FPTS, BR_i of a preemptive task (pi_1 > theta_i) can be affected by a higher priority task tau_h that cannot preempt it (theta_i >= pi_h > pi_i).

variables.BR_i: Best-case response time of task i
variables.pi_h: Priority of higher priority task h

formal_description.conclusion: Higher priority tasks that cannot preempt tau_i still influence its best-case response time.

informal_sketch.intuition: Even if a task tau_h cannot stop tau_i once tau_i starts, tau_h can delay the start of tau_i, which might push tau_i's execution into a window where it gets preempted by an even higher priority task.
steps: Observe task tau_3 with threshold that blocks tau_2 but not tau_1
Note that the presence of tau_2 changes the start time of tau_3
This change results in tau_3 being preempted by tau_1 differently
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_interference_fpts(task_i, task_set):
    # BR_i with all tasks
    br_full = calculate_BR_i(task_i, task_set)
    # BR_i without non-preempting HP tasks
    filtered_set = [t for t in task_set if not (task_i.theta >= t.pi > task_i.pi)]
    br_filtered = calculate_BR_i(task_i, filtered_set)
    return br_full != br_filtered
key_insights: FPTS lacks the independence from non-preempting tasks that FPNS enjoys.

formal_description.statement: In FPTS, a job k of task tau_i does not necessarily assume the BR_i when the activation of all higher priority tasks that can preempt tau_i coincides with the completion of job k.

variables.BR_i: Best-case response time of task i

formal_description.conclusion: The optimal instant for FPPS does not hold for FPTS.

informal_sketch.intuition: The 'optimal instant' logic from preemptive scheduling fails because the interaction between thresholds and multiple priority levels creates complex start-time dependencies.
steps: Apply the FPPS optimal instant phasing to an FPTS task set
Observe that another phasing yields a smaller response time
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def verify_fpps_instant_in_fpts(task_i, task_set):
    fpps_instant_R = simulate_at_fpps_optimal_instant(task_i, task_set)
    actual_BR = brute_force_BR(task_i, task_set)
    return actual_BR < fpps_instant_R
key_insights: FPTS analysis cannot be a simple extension of FPPS analysis.

formal_description.statement: In FPTS, the shortest response time of a task tau_i in a level-i active period is not necessarily assumed by the last job in that level-i active period.
formal_description.conclusion: The property that the last job in an active period is the 'best' (from FPPS) is invalidated in FPTS.

informal_sketch.intuition: In FPPS, the last job is best because it has the least 'carry-over' interference. In FPTS, the first job might be better because the threshold protection prevents preemptions that later jobs might suffer.
steps: Identify a level-i active period
Calculate response times for all jobs in that period
Find that the minimum is not the last job
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def check_best_job_position(task_i, active_period):
    jobs = active_period.get_jobs(task_i)
    best_job = min(jobs, key=lambda j: j.R_i_k)
    return best_job != jobs[-1]
key_insights: The non-duality between best-case and worst-case analysis is even more pronounced in FPTS.
